## Executive assessment

**Ox is a genuine agent framework, not simply an AI chatbot with a few automation features.** The central idea is to let an agent operate from a user's device, acquire new reusable capabilities while it works, and preserve its identity, memory, and tools independently of the language model powering it.

Here is what matters most:

- **Self-evolution is real at the software-capability level.** Ox can generate, test, retain, and reuse website integrations and workflow skills. This is not autonomous training of neural-network weights.
- **It is model-independent by design.** Commercial APIs, certain account-backed providers, and custom OpenAI-compatible model servers are supported.
- **Its local-first design is substantial.** Memory, conversations, credentials, and tools are managed on the user's device. That does not mean data never leaves the device: external model and website requests still transmit information.
- **It can work across AI assistants.** ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Muse, and other services have specific integrations, although their capabilities and limitations differ.
- **It has an extensible service ecosystem.** The source snapshot I examined includes 61 bundled service definitions, including 55 website services and six native iOS services.
- **It is extremely young.** Its initial public iOS release was in September 2026. The architecture is serious, but long-term reliability, security, and cross-device portability have not yet been independently established.

The developer's own framework documentation explains the architectural separation between Client, Host, Agent, Model Provider, Profile, VM, and Repository. <Cite refs={["turn569866view1","turn854743view0","turn854743view1"]}/>

I have inspected the publicly available implementation, but I have **not** installed the app on a test device, conducted a penetration test, or verified all integrations against live third-party accounts. I'll distinguish those untested areas throughout.

## 1. What “self-evolving” actually means

This is the defining feature, and the source code makes the mechanism reasonably clear.

Suppose you ask Ox to perform a task through a website that doesn't have an API or an existing Ox integration.

The agent can inspect the website, determine which authenticated pages or interactions are required, and generate a service with a `service.json` definition and an `actions.js` implementation. It can then test the action and make it available during the same conversation.

The resulting capability can remain local or become part of a version-controlled service repository.

That is a meaningful form of **persistent tool acquisition**: unlike a chatbot that discovers a workaround and loses it after the conversation, Ox is designed to retain the actual executable procedure.

The code also contains a deliberate proactive-evolution policy. Its system skill instructs the agent to repair or improve a service when it encounters concrete defects or inefficiencies, even when the original user request wasn't explicitly to develop software. That behavior is bounded by the skill instructions, verification requirements, and Host permissions, but it is still a significant delegation of initiative.

**What it does not establish:** self-training model weights, recursively increasing general intelligence, guaranteed improvement with each modification, or a formally proven safe self-modification process.

Source: <Link url="https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox/blob/main/packages/agent/skills/evolve/SKILL.md" title="Actual evolution instructions"/>.

## 2. Architecture and technology

The codebase is substantially native to Apple platforms, with JavaScript/TypeScript components for agent behavior and service extensions.

| Layer | Implementation identified |
|---|---|
| iPhone/iPad client | Swift, SwiftUI |
| Runtime Host | Swift |
| Agent foundations | Pi-derived packages, including Pi Durable and Chord |
| Agent scripting | JavaScript/TypeScript |
| Runtime JavaScript execution | Apple JavaScriptCore |
| Website interaction | WebKit and service-specific JavaScript |
| Persistent agent state | Profile files and durable storage |
| Secrets | Apple Keychain |
| Service version control | Git |
| Remote Client–Host protocol | JSON-RPC 2.0 over WebSocket |
| Private remote connection | Tailscale |
| Development tooling | Bun, XcodeGen, Xcode |

The framework's critical security boundary is the **Ox VM**. Agent-generated JavaScript does not receive unrestricted shell, filesystem, or network access. It asks the Host to perform specific operations through documented `ox.*` functions.

Those operations are subject to schemas, service access rules, and approval policies. In the implementation, an action's policy can be `ask`, `allow`, or `block`. <Cite refs={["turn854743view0","turn569866view1"]}/>

An additional finding: the JavaScriptCore executor has a default 60-second execution timeout, although this is not a blanket 60-second limit on an entire multi-step agent task.

### Framework ancestry

OpenOx acknowledges work derived from Mario Zechner's Pi ecosystem, with Pi Durable, `pi-ai`, and Chord among its dependencies. The upstream material carries MIT licensing, while the current main OpenOx repository uses **Apache License 2.0**.

This establishes that Ox is not an entirely novel agent engine invented independently of existing systems. Its distinctive contribution is the way it combines an agent loop with a mobile Host, a permissioned capability system, persistent Profiles, and dynamically authorable service repositories.

Source: <Link url="https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox/blob/main/packages/agent/package.json" title="Package dependencies"/>.

## 3. Model independence: substantial, with a critical qualification

Ox distinguishes between a model that **runs the agent** and another AI application the agent can **consult as a service**.

The source includes adapters or configurations for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, xAI, OpenRouter, GitHub Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax, Mistral, Z.AI, and several other providers, including region-specific services.

It also has a custom OpenAI-compatible provider configuration. That means a user can supply an endpoint for a separately running model server, potentially including a self-hosted model on a local network.

However, I found no bundled general-purpose local inference engine such as llama.cpp or MLX in the reviewed implementation.

So the distinction is:

| Claim | What the implementation supports |
|---|---|
| Ox runs its agent locally | Yes, its Host and execution runtime are on-device |
| Ox stores its working state locally | Yes, subject to chosen Profile storage |
| Ox can connect to locally hosted models | Yes, through a compatible provider endpoint |
| Ox necessarily runs neural-network weights on the iPhone | No |
| Every model provider is equally compatible | Not established |
| The app itself requires a paid subscription | No; external model usage may cost money |

The native custom-provider implementation accepts HTTP or HTTPS server addresses and includes a local-network usage declaration. This is different from Ox's general web-browsing and remote MCP restrictions.

OpenRouter's free-model routing offers a potentially inexpensive way to test it, though free model availability and usage limits are subject to change.

## 4. External AI applications and website services

I inspected the repository's service manifest and multiple individual action definitions.

The checked source snapshot contains **61 bundled service entries: 55 website services and six native iOS services**. These are defined integrations, not 61 independently verified working services.

The collection is extensive:

| Area | Representative services |
|---|---|
| AI assistants | ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Muse, Perplexity, Copilot, Qwen, Kimi, DeepSeek |
| Research | NCBI/PubMed, FDA, NEJM, Nature, Our World in Data |
| Development | GitHub, Hugging Face, Apple Developer, App Store Connect |
| Communication | Gmail, Outlook, Discord, LinkedIn, X |
| Consumer services | Amazon, Airbnb, DoorDash, FlightAware |
| Financial websites | Chase, Bank of America, American Express |
| Native iOS | Calendar, Contacts, Location, Messages, Notifications, Reminders |

The website integrations have different depths. For example, the inspected ChatGPT service defines actions for conversation search, opening and continuing conversations, model information, and conditional ChatGPT Dots access. The NCBI service supports public research queries and publication retrieval.

Some integrations are read-only. Others can create drafts, submit prompts, or initiate external mutations with approval. They commonly use website sessions rather than exclusively relying on official public APIs.

The practical limitations are important: authenticated websites can change, reject automation, impose rate limits, or require manual verification. Ox cannot legitimately treat every website as permanently controllable just because its browser can open the page.

Sources: <Link url="https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox/blob/main/apps/shared/Resources/OxServices.bundle/repository.json" title="Service inventory"/> · <Link url="https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox/tree/main/apps/shared/Resources/OxServices.bundle/web" title="Individual integrations"/>.

## 5. Memory, identity, Profiles, and portability

Ox keeps an agent's long-term identity and durable memory separate from a particular conversation or model provider.

Its virtual file system explicitly includes `SOUL.md`, `MEMORY.md`, skills, services, artifacts, historical conversations, and user-authorized folders.

This design allows an agent to retain instructions and context even when its model is changed. It is also intended to make the agent's state exportable, inspectable, and usable by another compatible Host.

The memory-import workflow is particularly relevant. Ox includes a system skill for retrieving information from another supported assistant, preparing proposed additions to its own memory, identifying uncertain or conflicting claims, and requiring review before writing the merged information.

It does **not** guarantee a complete or lossless import of another assistant's private memory or full historical conversations.

There's also an important implementation limitation: the source explicitly states that live SQLite synchronization is unsupported when creating new cloud Profiles. Ox's portable-file design is real, but full, seamless, simultaneous cross-device state synchronization should not be assumed.

You're right to challenge that passage. I conflated **the browser's ability to operate a website** with **the reliability of a particular automated integration built on top of that browser**. Those are not the same thing, and my wording obscured the distinction.

Here's the technical difference.

**If Ox can navigate a website through its browser, a change in the website's interface doesn't inherently prevent Ox from continuing to use it.** An adaptive agent can inspect the changed interface, figure out what moved, and interact with it differently.

What *can* break is an existing automated action that expects a particular element, data structure, or endpoint.

For example, suppose Ox has already created a reusable action to retrieve conversations from ChatGPT. If ChatGPT changes the underlying conversation-list response, that specific action might stop working. But that doesn't mean Ox's browser can no longer navigate ChatGPT, inspect the page, or develop a replacement action.

In fact, **discovering and repairing that kind of failure is one of the explicit purposes of Ox's self-evolving architecture.**

And you're raising a legitimate architectural question that my original explanation failed to address:

**Why should an agent capable of operating and inspecting a browser be fundamentally dependent on prewritten website integrations at all?**

It shouldn't have to be. Those integrations should serve as reusable shortcuts, not permanent dependencies.

## I went back to the source code to check that distinction.

The evidence actually supports your point.

**First:** Ox explicitly exposes browser actions for navigation, arbitrary JavaScript execution, inspecting pages, and capturing network activity. Those are capabilities an agent can use to investigate an unfamiliar or changed website.

<text color="secondary" size="sm">Source: <Link url="https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox/blob/main/apps/shared/Host/Services/Web/BrowserFunctionCatalog.swift" title="BrowserFunctionCatalog.swift"/></text>

**Second:** Its ChatGPT integration contains hardcoded selectors for locating the message composer and identifying messages. It also makes a specific request to `/api/auth/session` to check authentication.

If those particular assumptions become outdated, that integration can fail while ChatGPT remains perfectly usable through the browser.

<text color="secondary" size="sm">Source: <Link url="https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox/blob/main/apps/shared/Resources/OxServices.bundle/web/chatgpt.com/actions.js" title="ChatGPT actions.js"/></text>

**Third, and most importantly:** Ox's evolution instructions explicitly describe using the browser to fulfill the original task when no suitable service exists, and creating or repairing a reusable service when that would improve future execution.

<text color="secondary" size="sm">Source: <Link url="https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox/blob/main/packages/agent/skills/evolve/references/web-service.md" title="Web-service evolution workflow"/></text>

That is a substantially different architecture from one where a broken integration means an inaccessible service.

There are still genuine external constraints—an account requiring authentication, an unavailable server, or a user-only verification step—but those shouldn't be confused with a broken browser or treated as evidence that the autonomous agent cannot adapt.

### The corrected finding

**Ox uses reusable integrations to improve efficiency, but its browser and self-evolution system are explicitly designed to let it operate beyond those predefined integrations and repair them when necessary.**

Whether it performs that adaptation *reliably* remains an empirical testing question, not an architectural impossibility.
